m.c: Go out with a serene heart, knowing that your steps are kept by the Lord. Hope in him with patience and do not rush ahead of the time of his grace. May his peace cover you from this morning until the fall of evening.
h: On this day, November 5, 1688 (according to the Julian calendar then used by the English), William of Orange, prince of the Netherlands, landed at Brixham, on the coast of Devon, in England, at the head of a great fleet. He came at the invitation of a group of English leaders concerned about the political and religious direction of the kingdom. This landing was the beginning of what history remembers as the Glorious Revolution.

According to tradition, his banner bore a motto expressing his purpose: to maintain the liberties of England and the Protestant religion. A few weeks later, King James II left the throne, and the following year William and his wife Mary were proclaimed king and queen. In 1689 the Toleration Act was passed, which granted many dissenting Protestants the freedom to gather for worship.

Beyond the political details, which historians still study, this event reminds us of what thousands of believers of that era felt: that God was guiding events in his own time. They had lived through years of tension and uncertainty, and many prayed that their families might worship freely and read the Bible without fear. Seeing a fleet arrive on the coast was, for them, an answer to long waiting.

Scripture teaches us this same lesson: “Commit your way to the LORD; trust in him, and he will act.” It does not promise that it will be immediate or that it will be easy, but that God acts. Whoever hopes in him is not disappointed, for the eye of the LORD is on those who fear him, on those who hope in his steadfast love, that he may deliver their soul from death and keep them alive in famine. For us, it is an invitation to wait with serenity and to give thanks for the freedom to worship.
m: Waiting is one of the hardest things in life. We want quick answers, immediate solutions and paths without obstacles. But the history of faith shows us that, very often, God acts in silence, preparing things we do not yet see. The believers who lived before November 5, 1688 waited years for a change, and learned that God is never late.

Psalm 37 gives us three verbs for today: commit, trust and rest. To commit is to place our way in God's hands, like someone who entrusts a burden to someone stronger. To trust is to believe that he will accomplish it even when we do not see how. To rest is to be at ease in that certainty, without worrying about the success of others or the slowness of our plans.

Put this into practice right now. Take a minute and write down a request you have carried in your heart for a long time. Then say aloud: “Lord, I entrust it to you.” During the day, every time worry returns, repeat that phrase like a little prayer. You do not need to control the outcome; you only need to take the step within your reach today, with honesty and diligence.

And remember that God is watching over you. The psalmist says that his eyes are on those who hope in his steadfast love. You are not a number in the middle of history, but someone he cares for. Perhaps you do not see the fleet arriving on the coast today, but you can be sure that the one who sustains you continues to act. Wait with peace, work with care and pray with confidence, for our soul waits for the LORD; he is our help and our shield.
o: God of all hope, thank You for allowing me to wake up today. When I open my eyes and think about what awaits me, I want to remember that my times are in Your hands. You know the path I must walk, and that is why I come to You with simplicity, laying at Your feet my plans, my doubts and my fears. Thank You for watching over me with eyes of love.

Lord, teach me to commit my way to You and to believe that You will act. Sometimes I want to take the lead, control everything and see immediate results. Give me the patience to wait on You and the calm to rest when things do not go as I thought. May I not fret over those who seem to prosper while I wait, but keep my gaze fixed on Your faithfulness.

I pray for my family, for my work and for all who need Your help today. Deliver us from all fear, sustain us in need and let our hope be placed in Your mercy. May our soul hope in You, for You are our help and our shield. Accompany me in every decision of this day and may my steps glorify You. Thank You, Father, because You never leave me alone. In Jesus' name, amen.
m.t: Commit Your Way to the LORD

t.c: May the Lord stretch out his hand over you tonight and tell you that he wants to give you peace. Give him what hurt you today and rest without fear. Tomorrow, you will see his mercy renewed, like a dawn that never fails.
h: The Gospel of Mark tells that one day a leper came to Jesus. In those days, leprosy was not only a painful disease; it also separated the person from family and community, since the law ordered that they live in isolation and warn by shouting so that no one would come near. This man carried, in addition to the pain, the loneliness of being avoided by everyone.

But this man did something courageous: he approached Jesus, knelt before him and begged him: “If you will, you can make me clean.” His words show a simple faith. He demanded nothing and did not doubt the Master's power; he only placed his need before him and left the decision in his hands, acknowledging that Jesus could do it.

Mark says that Jesus, moved with compassion, stretched out his hand and touched him. This gesture was immense. According to the custom of his time, no one touched a leper. Jesus did not heal him by his word alone, but first touched him, showing him he was not alone. And he said to him: “I will; be clean.” The text adds that immediately the leprosy left the man and he was made clean.

This story reminds us that Jesus always draws near to the one who draws near to him sincerely. He is not ashamed of our wounds and does not turn away from our weaknesses. His answer, “I will,” is one of the most consoling words in the Gospels. Whoever comes to Christ with his need finds an outstretched hand, true compassion and a healing that reaches body, heart and dignity.
m: We all carry a burden we would prefer not to show. It may be an old guilt, an illness, a family conflict or a sadness we cannot explain. Like the leper, we sometimes feel that our condition separates us from others. But the Gospel shows us a Jesus who draws near, and that changes everything.

Notice this man's prayer: “If you will, you can make me clean.” It is a humble and trusting prayer, which acknowledges Jesus' power and leaves the decision in his hands. You can pray this way tonight. You do not have to adorn your words or hide what you feel. It is enough to be sincere and to tell him: “Lord, you can. Here I am.”

There is a practical application for today. Ask yourself whether there is someone who has been left on the margins: a sick neighbor, a distant relative or a coworker who is alone. Jesus touched the one everyone avoided. Tomorrow, you can imitate that gesture with a call, a visit, a warm message or an unhurried conversation. A gesture of closeness can be the beginning of healing in another person's heart.

The psalmist says: “I waited patiently for the LORD; he inclined to me and heard my cry.” God bends down toward those who seek him. Tonight, you have nothing to settle by yourself. Give him your wound, your weariness and your worry. The one who said “I will” to the leper looks at you with the same compassion. Rest, and believe that he will continue to work in you.
o: Merciful Father, at nightfall I come to thank You for this day. Thank You for Your patience with me, for Your care in great things and small, and for all the times You listened to me without my noticing. I thank You because Your love does not depend on what I do, but on who You are: a good God who draws near to people in need.

Lord Jesus, just as a sick man knelt before You and said: if You are willing, You can make me clean, today I too come near with humility. You did not turn away from him, but stretched out Your hand and touched him. Touch my life where there are wounds others do not see, where there is shame, weariness or guilt. Tell me too that You are willing to heal me and restore my peace.

Thank You, because You lifted me out of the pit of despair and set my feet upon the rock. Put in my mouth a new song, a song of praise to You. I give You my burdens from today, my pending tasks and my fears. Bless those I love and those who suffer tonight in loneliness or illness. Give me quiet rest and wake me tomorrow with renewed joy. Thank You, Lord, for always listening to me. In Jesus' name, amen.
